query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small fraction of metallic silver (Ag) as a ductile binder phase into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy matrix will significantly improve mechanical integrity (compressive strength and resistance to cracking) without sacrificing the rare-earth-free status or substantially diminishing the caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, rare-earth-free, brittle, large caloric response
generation.intervention: Add 5–10 vol% metallic Ag as a binder phase via powder metallurgy or melt infiltration
generation.conditions: Applied magnetic field (up to 2 T), hydrostatic pressure (up to 1 GPa), temperature range 250–350 K, compressive loading up to 200 MPa
generation.structural_mediator: Ag forms a continuous or semi-continuous ductile network at grain boundaries, bridging cracks and distributing stress
generation.mechanism: Ag binder increases ductility and toughness by arresting crack propagation and redistributing local stresses, while its high thermal conductivity aids heat transport. Ag does not strongly interact magnetically, so the caloric response is preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compressive strength increases by at least 50% relative to the unmodified alloy (expected >150 MPa), crack resistance improves, and caloric response (ΔS, ΔT) remains within 90% of baseline. Thermal conductivity increases moderately compared to epoxy composites.
generation.baseline: Unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy: poor mechanical integrity, large caloric response, rare-earth-free
generation.boundary: Intervention effective for Ag content up to 10 vol%; higher contents may dilute caloric effect. Must avoid rare-earth elements. Performance assessed under applied fields, pressure, and temperature as specified.
generation.uncertainty: Exact impact on caloric response is uncertain; possible minor reduction due to binder phase, but expected to remain high. Ag distribution and interface quality may affect mechanical gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples with 0, 5, and 10 vol% Ag binder via powder metallurgy. Measure compressive strength, crack resistance, caloric response (ΔS, ΔT) under applied magnetic field and pressure, and thermal conductivity. Compare to baseline alloy and prior epoxy/In composites.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if Ag addition fails to increase compressive strength by at least 50% or if caloric response drops below 80% of baseline value.
